newsitem.title: UK: Electricity watchdog sets cost recovery guidelines.
newsitem.headline: Electricity watchdog sets cost recovery guidelines.

text.p: British electricity watchdog Offer on Tuesday issued a consultation paper about the charges which public electricity suppliers (PESs) may make to recover the costs of providing certain services in order to facilitate competition in supply after 1998.

Offer Director General Stephen Littlechild set out alternative assumptions on which each company's allowance should be set. At the lower end, the average allowance would be 18 million pounds per company spread over five years, ranging from 12 million to 26 million depending on size of company. At the higher end, the average allowance would be 27 million pounds, spread over five years, with a range from 16 million to 34 million.

"Public electricity suppliers will be required to provide certain new services from 1998. These will justify additional revenue, but only to the extent that the costs involved are reasonable," Littlechild said.
He said PESs have argued that the cost of providing data management services will be much higher than they originally estimated.

"In my view, an allowance of about one-third to one-half of the cost estimates made by the companies would be reasonable. This should not exceed around one percent of a typical domestic customer's bill," Littlechild said.

Offer said the paper is a report on work in progress rather than a set of final proposals. It said the PESs' business plan estimates of these data management services costs amount to some 850 million stg over five years, some five to six times the level envisaged in Offer's September 1996 consultation paper.
It said there is "great variation" between companies' estimates, ranging from under 35 million pounds to over 115 million.
